scams.name: Memphis Red-Light Camera & Fake Traffic Ticket Mail Scam
scams.description:
Memphis has a mix of real city-operated red-light camera tickets (legitimate, $50) and scam mailed "traffic tickets" that target out-of-state visitors two to six weeks after a Memphis trip. The scam comes in several variants: (1) an official-looking mailed "notice of violation" with a URL that directs to a scam payment site (legitimate tickets are paid at memphistn.gov only); (2) a demand for $150-$300 for an "unpaid red-light violation plus late fees" when no violation actually occurred; (3) aggressive follow-up calls threatening that a "warrant" has been issued if payment is not made; and (4) "DMV action" threats aimed at out-of-state drivers. Phishing patterns impersonating the Tennessee DMV circulate as well, and new variants keep appearing.

For older travelers who drove in Memphis and received a mailed "traffic ticket," the protective playbook is straightforward: (1) verify that the ticket is real by checking the memphistn.gov traffic-violations search with the citation number — if it doesn't appear, it's a scam; (2) remember that legitimate Memphis red-light camera tickets cost $50, so a ticket "plus $250 late fees" within weeks of the supposed infraction is a scam red flag; (3) pay real tickets only at memphistn.gov or by mail to the Memphis Traffic Violations Bureau — never through URLs in the mailing; (4) know that the Tennessee Department of Safety (TN DMV) does not suspend out-of-state licenses for Memphis traffic tickets, so "warrant issued" threats are 100% fake; (5) if you receive a "TN DMV" email claiming license suspension, delete it — the TN DMV does not email license actions; and (6) report phishing attempts to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
scams.avoidance: Verify any ticket at the memphistn.gov traffic-violations search. Real Memphis red-light tickets cost $50 (not $150-$300 with "late fees"). Pay real tickets only at memphistn.gov or by mail to the Traffic Violations Bureau. The TN DMV does not email license suspensions — delete phishing. Report phishing to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
scams.location: Downtown Memphis traffic corridors, Summer Ave / Poplar Ave intersections, out-of-state Memphis travelers receiving mailed 'tickets'
scams.tldr: Memphis mixes real $50 city red-light camera tickets with scam mailed "traffic tickets" sent to out-of-state visitors two to six weeks after their trip, demanding $150-$300 in fake fines and late fees via bogus payment URLs, with threatening follow-up calls. Verify any citation at memphistn.gov before paying.

scams.name: Beale Street Parking & Downtown Memphis Parking Scam
scams.description:
Unauthorized "parking attendants" demand cash on residential streets near Beale Street, and several related schemes work the downtown area. The patterns include: (1) unauthorized individuals in reflective vests demanding $10-$20 cash on residential streets near Beale, claiming an "attendant parking" service that doesn't exist; (2) fake "parking ticket" URLs left on windshields that lead to scam sites (legitimate Memphis tickets are paid at memphistn.gov); (3) a "premium Beale Street VIP lot" that is privately operated at $25-$40 a night without clear signage; and (4) "event weekend" surge pricing on private lots at $50-$80 per night during Grizzlies games, Elvis Week, and music festivals. Legitimate options include the Peabody Place Parking Garage ($10 flat rate), the Second Street Garage ($12), the AutoZone Park lot ($10 for concerts and games), and free street parking on Second Street on Sundays.

For older travelers visiting downtown Memphis, the clean playbook is this: (1) use the official downtown garages — Peabody Place ($10), Second Street ($12), and the AutoZone Park lot ($10 on event days) — all of which have digital pay stations and posted rates; (2) refuse unauthorized "parking attendants" in reflective vests on residential streets, as they have no legal authority; (3) for Beale Street specifically, use the Peabody Place Garage, which is two blocks away and well-lit at night; (4) if you find a "parking ticket" with a URL on your windshield, verify it at memphistn.gov before paying, since windshield-URL citations are commonly fakes; and (5) for weekend events such as Grizzlies games, Elvis Week, and the Beale Street Music Festival, pre-book parking through the ParkMobile app at the Peabody Place or Second Street Garage and avoid the "event weekend" private lots charging $50 or more.
scams.avoidance: Use the official garages: Peabody Place ($10), Second Street ($12), and AutoZone Park ($10). Refuse "parking attendants" on residential streets — they have no legal authority. Pre-book through ParkMobile for weekend events. Verify any windshield "ticket" at memphistn.gov before paying. Peabody Place is two blocks from Beale with a well-lit walk.
scams.location: Beale Street downtown parking, Second Street paid lots, Front Street riverfront parking, Memphis Pyramid / Bass Pro area
scams.tldr: Near Beale Street, unauthorized "attendants" in reflective vests demand $10-$20 cash for parking that doesn't exist, fake windshield "ticket" URLs lead to scam sites, and private lots gouge $50-$80 on event weekends. Use official garages like Peabody Place ($10) and Second Street ($12) instead.

scams.name: Memphis MEM Airport Rideshare & 'Early Morning Uber' Scam
scams.description:
At Memphis International Airport (MEM), travelers encounter rideshare overcharges and early-morning Uber and Lyft reliability problems. MEM is 10 miles from downtown Memphis, and legitimate fares run $18-$32 by Uber or Lyft depending on surge (with pickup at the designated rideshare zone in MEM Economy Parking), or $32-$42 for a licensed taxi with the meter running. The scam variants include: (1) drivers at baggage claim offering a "flat $50" to downtown when the metered fare is $32-$42; (2) "limo" touts quoting $80 or more for standard trips; (3) unreliable Uber and Lyft availability between 4 and 6 a.m. for early flights, when drivers occasionally cancel after confirming and leave travelers stranded (not a scam as such, but a MEM reality check); (4) "shuttle" touts offering a "downtown shuttle" for $40 when Uber is $20; and (5) drivers demanding a cash tip beyond the app total.

For older travelers arriving at MEM, the clean playbook is this: (1) take Uber or Lyft from the rideshare pickup in MEM Economy Parking with a fare screenshot ($18-$32 to downtown); (2) use a licensed taxi with the meter running at the official taxi queue ($32-$42 to downtown); (3) consider MATA Route 2, the airport bus, at $1.75 (schedule-limited, but scam-proof); (4) for early-morning departures from Memphis between 4 and 6 a.m., book Uber Reserve 24 or more hours in advance through the Uber app to reduce cancellation risk; (5) refuse drivers soliciting at baggage claim with "flat" rates; (6) never pay a cash tip beyond the Uber app total, since app tips are already processed; and (7) for the trip from Memphis to Nashville (200 miles), a rental car is the most reliable option — Greyhound is $25, and Amtrak does not serve the Memphis-Nashville route.
scams.avoidance: Take Uber or Lyft from the MEM Economy Parking rideshare zone with a fare screenshot. A licensed metered taxi runs $32-$42 to downtown. MATA Route 2 airport bus is $1.75 (schedule-limited). Book Uber Reserve 24-plus hours ahead for 4-6 a.m. departures. Refuse cash-tip demands beyond the app total.
scams.location: Memphis International Airport (MEM) baggage claim, rideshare pickup zone (MEM Economy Parking), licensed taxi queue
scams.tldr: At MEM (10 miles from downtown), drivers at baggage claim push "flat $50" rides when the metered fare is $32-$42, and early-morning (4-6 a.m.) Uber and Lyft pickups are notoriously unreliable. Use the official rideshare zone in Economy Parking with a fare screenshot, and book Uber Reserve ahead for early departures.

scams.name: Graceland Tour Package Upsell & Historic-Site Ticket Scam
scams.description:
Graceland (Elvis Presley's estate, 3764 Elvis Presley Blvd) is a major tourist destination with legitimate tiered pricing: the Essential Tour at $48 for adults, the Elvis Experience Tour at $65 for adults, and the Ultimate VIP Tour at $185 for adults, all bookable at graceland.com. The scam variants include: (1) third-party "Graceland VIP" resellers charging $80-$150 for the $48 Essential Tour; (2) hotel-concierge "Graceland packages" that include a shuttle at $95 or more per person, even though Graceland offers a free shuttle from its visitor center and the Sun Studio shuttle is $15; (3) "Elvis Experience" upsell packages at $250 or more per person when the actual Elvis Experience Tour is $65; and (4) inflated Airbnb and hotel pricing during the Elvis Birthday Celebration week (January 8-12) and Elvis Week (August 10-16). For cultural context, Graceland itself was the target of a separate 2024 foreclosure-fraud attempt — not a visitor scam, but a sign of how often the name attracts fraud.

For older travelers visiting Graceland, the clean playbook is this: (1) book Graceland tickets only at graceland.com or at the Graceland visitor center ticket booth, where the $48 Essential Tour is the genuine base rate; (2) use the free shuttle Graceland offers from the visitor center to the Mansion (included in admission); (3) for Sun Studio ($15, an 8-minute walk from most downtown hotels), book direct at sunstudio.com rather than through "Memphis Music package" resellers charging $50 or more; (4) for the Memphis Rock 'n' Soul Museum ($12), the Stax Museum of American Soul Music ($14), and the National Civil Rights Museum at the Lorraine Motel ($18), book direct at each official site; (5) for Elvis Week (August) or the Birthday Celebration (January), book hotels four or more months ahead to avoid inflated last-minute pricing; and (6) pay by credit card for chargeback leverage if any package fails to deliver.
scams.avoidance: Book Graceland tickets only at graceland.com or the visitor center booth: $48 Essential Tour. Graceland offers a free shuttle from the visitor center to the Mansion. Book Sun Studio direct at sunstudio.com ($15) and skip Memphis Music resellers. Book the Rock 'n' Soul, Stax, and National Civil Rights museums direct at each site. For Elvis Week or the Birthday Celebration, book hotels four-plus months ahead.
scams.location: Graceland visitor plaza, hotel-concierge Graceland tour desks, online third-party 'Graceland VIP' resellers, Memphis Airbnb concierge services
scams.tldr: Graceland's real ticket prices start at $48 (Essential Tour), but third-party resellers charge $80-$150 for it, hotel concierges add $95-plus shuttle packages, and "Elvis Experience" upsells hit $250-plus. Book only at graceland.com or the visitor center, and use Graceland's free Mansion shuttle.

scams.name: Memphis Downtown Panhandling, Gold Chain Hustle & Beale Street Aggressive Solicitation
scams.description:
Downtown Memphis sees elevated panhandling activity, including a recurring gold-chain hustle in which a man approaches tourists and tries to sell a "dropped" gold-plated chain for $40-$100, claiming it's "real gold" when it's actually plated zinc alloy worth less than $5. The variants include: (1) a "dropped wallet" scam in which a wallet "dropped" nearby is paired with an accusation of theft; (2) aggressive panhandlers pressuring people for $5-$20 with sob stories; (3) a "ride assistance" ploy in which a stranger offers to "help you find your Uber" and then demands a $10-plus tip; and (4) broader downtown safety concerns that are well documented. Similar scam patterns also turn up at Wolfchase Mall in the suburbs.

For older travelers in downtown Memphis, and especially on Beale Street, the defensive playbook is this: (1) give a firm "no thank you" to all unsolicited approaches and keep walking — do not engage in conversation about dropped items, "help," or "stories"; (2) refuse any "gold chain" or jewelry offered by a stranger, as these are plated zinc worth less than $5 in material value; (3) if someone claims you "took their wallet," walk toward the nearest Memphis Police officer (Beale Street has visible patrols) and do not hand over anything; (4) note that Beale Street has a $5 cover charge after 10 p.m. on weekends (legitimate, enforced by city police at the entry points), but any "additional entertainment tax" collected by anyone other than the official gates is a scam; (5) keep in mind that Memphis PD's non-emergency line is 901-545-2677, downtown patrol is visible, and 911 is for active threats; and (6) walk in pairs after dark, especially between Beale Street and your parked car or hotel.
scams.avoidance: Give a firm "no thank you" and keep walking — no conversation. Refuse all "gold chain" offers — zinc alloy worth under $5. If accused of "taking a wallet," walk toward the visible Beale Street police. Beale Street's official $5 cover after 10 p.m. on weekends is legitimate — no other fees are. Memphis PD non-emergency: 901-545-2677; walk in pairs after dark.
scams.location: Beale Street (Second to Third), downtown Memphis sidewalks near Peabody Hotel, Tom Lee Park, Main Street Trolley stops
scams.tldr: Downtown Memphis, especially Beale Street, has heavy panhandling and a gold-chain hustle where a stranger sells a "dropped" plated-zinc chain (worth under $5) as real gold for $40-$100, sometimes paired with a "you took my wallet" accusation. Give a firm "no thank you," refuse the chain, and keep walking.

scams.name: Memphis 'Wolfchase' Mall & Suburban Retail-Area Check Scam
scams.description:
At Wolfchase Galleria and other suburban Memphis malls, a scam pattern targets older shoppers in several ways: (1) a "good Samaritan" approaches after spotting a shopper at the register, "helps" bag items, then uses sleight of hand to swap cash or reach into a wallet; (2) a "distraction" pair, in which one person strikes up a conversation while the other shoplifts the victim's shopping bag; (3) an "I need you to cash this check for me" play aimed at older retirees with what looks like a legitimate check ($800-$2,500) — the check bounces two weeks later and the "cash" handed to the stranger is gone; and (4) "charity collection" in the mall parking lot, soliciting $20 or more in cash for fake nonprofits. Related patterns appear across suburban Memphis.

For older travelers shopping at Wolfchase or other Memphis suburban malls, the protective playbook is this: (1) never accept help from strangers at checkout registers — politely decline with "I have it, thank you"; (2) keep your shopping bag on your person, not on the cart, and never leave it in restaurants or bathroom stalls; (3) refuse any request to "cash a check" for a stranger, no matter how legitimate it appears, because such checks bounce and real check-cashing requires bank verification; (4) refuse all "mall parking lot charity" cash solicitations, since legitimate nonprofits don't collect this way; (5) if you feel followed or targeted, walk directly to mall security or any open retail store; (6) remember that the non-emergency line for the Wolfchase area is 901-545-2677; and (7) shop with a companion when possible, as it's easier to be targeted alone.
scams.avoidance: Decline all checkout help from strangers: "I have it, thank you." Keep shopping bags on your person, not on the cart. Refuse all "cash this check" requests — the checks bounce. Refuse parking-lot charity cash — real nonprofits don't collect that way. Walk to mall security if you feel targeted or followed.
scams.location: Wolfchase Galleria (suburban Memphis), Oak Court Mall, Agricenter area retail, Cordova retail strips
scams.tldr: At Wolfchase Galleria and other suburban Memphis malls, scammers target older shoppers with checkout "helpers" who swap cash, distraction pairs who steal bags, fake parking-lot charities, and an "cash this check for me" con using checks that bounce two weeks later. Decline all stranger help and never cash a check for anyone.
